what_it_does: Every time a modern processor runs a program, it tries to predict in advance which way each 'if' branch will go so it can keep working ahead of time rather than stalling. Standard branch predictors take several clock cycles to make that prediction, which is too slow for aggressive ahead-of-time prediction. Ahead prediction solves the latency problem by starting even earlier, but the naive approach has to consider all possible combinations of the next several branches — 2 raised to the power of N paths, which multiplies energy use by 14.6 times and is impractical. This paper observes that in real programs only one or two of those many possible history patterns actually occur at runtime; the rest are theoretical ghosts. By modifying the TAGE predictor (a well-known prediction table design) to track only patterns that actually appear, the method cuts the energy overhead from 14.6 times down to just 1.5 times while still delivering a 4.4% throughput improvement.
